extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)/(c)/(d) doctrines: on-sale and public-use bars, the experimental-use exception, abandonment (102(c)), and foreign-priority bars (102(d)). Intended to instruct examiners how to evaluate facts (sales, testing, disclosures, foreign filings) against statutory bars and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pfaff on-sale bar test (two prongs)
rubrics_metrics.description: "[T]he on-sale bar applies when two conditions are satisfied before the critical date [more than one year before the effective filing date of the claimed invention]. First, the product must be the subject of a commercial offer for sale…. Second, the invention must be ready for patenting."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pfaff v. Wells (quoted). Both prongs must be satisfied before the critical date to trigger the pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) on-sale bar. See Invitrogen Corp. v. Biocrest for application to public use as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ready for patenting — two alternative proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: "'Ready for patenting' ... may be satisfied in at least two ways: by proof of reduction to practice before the critical date; or by proof that prior to the critical date the inventor had prepared drawings or other descriptions of the invention that were sufficiently specific to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If detailed drawings/specifications available pre-critical date enable a skilled person to make the claimed invention, the invention can be 'ready for patenting' even absent reduction to practice. Cases: Pfaff (computer chip socket), Weatherchem (plastic dispensing caps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual reduction to practice before sale bars patent
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention was actually reduced to practice before being sold or offered for sale more than 1 year before filing of the application, a patent will be barred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual reduction to practice typically requires testing under actual working conditions demonstrating practical utility, unless the invention's simplicity makes operativeness clear. Cases: Vanmoor v. Wal-Mart; Field v. Knowles; Steinberg v. Seitz; In re Hamilton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product embodying all claim limitations triggers on-sale bar
rubrics_metrics.description: "If a product that is offered for sale inherently possesses each of the limitations of the claims, then the invention is on sale, whether or not the parties to the transaction recognize that the product possesses the claimed characteristics."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjective ignorance of particular properties by parties does not avoid the on-sale bar (Abbott Laboratories; STX v. Brine). Even subjective qualities inherent in a product cannot be an escape hatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar does not require market-ready/satisfactory commercial marketing
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention need not be ready for satisfactory commercial marketing for sale to bar a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Atlantic Thermoplastics Co. v. Faytex Corp. Thus, lack of commercial polish or readiness for broad marketing does not prevent an on-sale bar if the Pfaff prongs are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of a process — know-how vs. sale/performance
rubrics_metrics.description: "'Know-how' describing what the process consists of and how the process should be carried out may be sold ... However, such a transaction is not a 'sale' of the invention within the meaning of [pre-AIA] §102(b) because the process has not been carried out or performed as a result of the transaction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sale of know-how alone is generally not an on-sale bar for a claimed method. But sale of a product made by the claimed process, an offer to perform the claimed process, or a device embodying the claimed method may trigger the bar. Cases: In re Kollar; D.L. Auld; Scaltech; Minton. Sale of a prior-art device different from the claimed device does not trigger the bar unless it actually practices the claimed method before the critical date (Poly-America).

rubrics_metrics.name: "In this country" geographic scope
rubrics_metrics.description: "The language 'in this country' in pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) does not include other WTO or NAFTA member countries, but includes any State of the United States, the District of Columbia, and any commonwealth, territory, or possession of the United States."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public use or on-sale activity must take place in the United States to trigger the pre-AIA 102(b) bars in general. Manufacture and delivery both in a foreign country generally do not create an on-sale bar, but substantial prefatory activity in the U.S. or offers for sale originating in the U.S. may suffice (Gandy; Robbins; CTS Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental-use doctrine — primary-purpose test
rubrics_metrics.description: The question posed by the experimental use doctrine is 'whether the primary purpose of the inventor at the time of the sale, as determined from an objective evaluation of the facts surrounding the transaction, was to conduct experimentation.' Experimentation must be the primary purpose and any commercial exploitation must be incidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If experimentation is the primary purpose, the sale/use is not a bar. Market testing or attempts to gauge consumer demand are commercial, not experimental. Key cases: Allen Eng'g Corp. v. Bartell; EZ Dock; LaBounty; In re Smith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy against commercial exploitation more than one year before filing
rubrics_metrics.description: One policy of the on sale and public use bars is the prevention of inventors from exploiting their inventions commercially more than 1 year prior to the filing of a patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where bona fide experimental activity exists, an inventor may not commercially exploit an invention more than one year prior to the filing date. Case: In re Theis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial activity must legitimately advance development; burden increases with exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: As the degree of commercial exploitation surrounding pre-AIA 102(b) activity increases, the burden on an applicant to establish clear and convincing evidence of experimental activity ... will rarely be met unless clear and convincing necessity for the experimentation is established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should carefully scrutinize objective facts where alleged experimental activity occurs in a commercial atmosphere. Even a sale can be justified if it legitimately advances experimental development, but objective evidence is essential. Cases: Theis; Robbins Co.; Ushakoff; Cloud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicia of commercial exploitation (A–F)
rubrics_metrics.description: The following activities should be used by the examiner as indicia of this subjective intent: (A) Preparation of commercial documents (orders, invoices, receipts, delivery schedules); (B) Preparation of price lists and distribution of price quotations; (C) Display of samples to prospective customers; (D) Demonstration of models or prototypes (especially at trade conventions); (E) Use of an invention where an admission fee is charged; (F) Advertising in publicity releases, brochures, and various periodicals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors are examples of objective evidence that the activity was commercial exploitation rather than experimentation; see cited cases for each indicium. See MPEP § 2133.03(e)(4) for experimental-purpose factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent where sales in ordinary commercial environment
rubrics_metrics.description: "When sales are made in an ordinary commercial environment and the goods are placed outside the inventor's control, an inventor's secretly held subjective intent to 'experiment,' even if true, is unavailing without objective evidence to support the contention. ... the customer at a minimum must be made aware of the experimentation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secret subjective belief is insufficient if the transaction looks like ordinary commercial sales and the inventor relinquished control. Cases: LaBounty; Harrington; Paragon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of the invention — when experimental use ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental use 'means perfecting or completing an invention to the point of determining that it will work for its intended purpose.' Therefore, experimental use 'ends with an actual reduction to practice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inventor was satisfied the invention was 'complete,' later activities (e.g., awaiting approval) normally will not revive experimental use. Lack of specific modifications from experimentation is evidence (not conclusive) that activity was not experimental. Disposal of a prototype after completion without restraints constitutes a bar. Cases: RCA; Interroyal; Skil; In re Blaisdell; In re Theis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors indicative of experimental purpose (13-factor list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have considered numerous factors to determine if a sale was primarily for experimentation: (1) necessity for public testing, (2) amount of control retained by inventor, (3) nature of the invention, (4) length of the test period, (5) whether payment was made, (6) whether there was a secrecy obligation, (7) whether records of the experiment were kept, (8) who conducted the experiment, (9) the degree of commercial exploitation during testing, (10) whether the invention reasonably requires evaluation under actual conditions of use, (11) whether testing was systematically performed, (12) whether the inventor continually monitored the invention during testing, and (13) the nature of contacts made with potential customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customer's awareness of testing is a critical attribute. No single or particular combination of factors is necessarily determinative; examiner must evaluate scope and length of activity relative to nature of the subject matter. Cases: Allen Eng'g; EZ Dock; Electromotive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision/control during third-party testing
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor must maintain sufficient control over the invention during testing by third parties; extent of supervision and customer awareness are significant determinative factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inventor relinquishes supervision/control without restraints and allows unrestricted use, that relinquishment can create a statutory bar. Cases: Electromotive; In re Blaisdell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted experimental activity — developmental testing and utility determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Testing of an invention in the normal context of its technological development is generally within the realm of permitted experimental activity. Experimentation to determine utility may also be permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., continued testing of a chemical composition with no known utility is likely permissible absent sale or other commercial exploitation. However, market testing to gauge acceptance and testing to appease customers or minor tune-ups (not needing inventor's skill) are not permitted. Cases: General Motors v. Bendix; Smith & Davis; In re Theis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market testing is not experimental use
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The experimental use exception...does not include market testing where the inventor is attempting to gauge consumer demand for his claimed invention. The purpose of such activities is commercial exploitation and not experimentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market testing, consumer-demand trials, and activities aimed at product acceptance are treated as commercial, not experimental, and can create a statutory bar. Case: In re Smith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental activity in design applications — ornament vs. functional testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use of an ornamental design directed toward generating consumer interest in aesthetics is not an experimental use; experimentation directed to functional features of a product containing an ornamental design may negate public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design-display for consumer interest typically creates public use; functional testing of features may be experimental if properly controlled. Cases: In re Mann; Tone Brothers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental-use exception is personal to the applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory bars ... are applicable even though public use or on sale activity is by a party other than an applicant. Evidence of experimental activity by such other party will not overcome a prima facie case unless the activity was under the supervision and control of the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities of independent third parties do not confer the applicant the benefit of the experimental-use exception absent applicant control/supervision. Cases: In re Hamilton; Magnetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c) — abandonment requires intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. 102(c), abandonment of the 'invention' results in loss of right to a patent. 'Actual abandonment under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c) requires that the inventor intend to abandon the invention, and intent can be implied from the inventor's conduct with respect to the invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent must be deliberate (implied or express); delay alone is not sufficient to infer abandonment. Delay in reapplying after abandoning an earlier application does not automatically constitute abandonment. Disclosure without claiming in prior issued patent is rebuttable by a later-filed application. Only in priority contests will lapse of time bar a patent (see MPEP § 2138.03). Cases: In re Gibbs; Ex parte Dunne; Lovell v. Peer; Moore v. United States; Davis Harvester; Petersen v. Fee Int'l.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) — foreign-filed patent/inventor's-certificate bar (four conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) establishes four conditions which, if all are present, establish a statutory bar: (A) foreign application filed more than 12 months before the effective U.S. filing date; (B) same applicant (or legal representatives/assigns) for both filings; (C) the foreign application must have actually issued as a patent or inventor's certificate before the U.S. filing; (D) the same invention must be involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a foreign patent/inventor's-certificate satisfying these four requirements is discovered, the examiner makes a rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d). See MPEP § 2135.01 for searching and clarification of each requirement.
